tagline: A distraction-free Markdown library where the whole manuscript lives in one place.
verdictSummary: Ulysses has no model, no service and no network dependency: it is a well-made writing environment over a library of Markdown sheets, with filters, goals and export. Every one of those parts is buildable in a sitting, and the result is genuinely usable. What you are not buying back is the craftsmanship — iCloud sync that never loses a sheet, an iPad app, and export through templates that produce a book-quality PDF.
coreLoopDIY: Keep every piece of writing as a Markdown sheet in one searchable library, organise with groups and saved filters instead of folders, set a word target per sheet, and export to DOCX, EPUB or PDF.
whatYouLose: iCloud sync and the iPad and iPhone apps
the export style system that produces publication-ready documents
direct publishing to WordPress, Ghost and Medium
a decade of small interactions being exactly right
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a writing app is judged on the thousandth hour, not the first. Six dollars a month for something that has never lost a sheet is a rational trade for anyone who writes for a living.
notes: No AI anywhere: upstream's draft attached a grammar-checker prompt, which describes a different product. Ulysses is a writing environment, and the honest rebuild has no API key at all.
prompt:
Build a Markdown writing environment organised as one library of sheets. No AI, no network calls, no account.

Library model: a sheet is a Markdown file. Sheets live in groups, and groups nest. There is no separate document-open step — the library is always the left column, and clicking a sheet edits it. A sheet's title is its first heading, not a filename.

Filters, which replace folders: a saved filter is a query over the library (contains text, has tag, modified within N days, word count above or below a threshold, in group X including subgroups). Filters appear in the sidebar alongside groups and update live. This is what makes a flat library scale past a few hundred sheets.

Editor: Markdown with inline styling shown rather than raw syntax where possible — bold renders bold while the asterisks stay editable. Typewriter scrolling, a focus mode that dims everything except the current paragraph or sentence, and a full-screen mode with no interface at all. Keyboard shortcuts for every navigation action; the mouse should be optional.

Goals: a per-sheet or per-group target in words, characters or pages, with a deadline. Show a ring that fills as you write and a session count of words added today. Store a daily writing history so a streak and a chart are possible.

Attachments per sheet: notes, keywords, and images, held in a right-hand column that can be hidden.

Export: compile a selection of sheets, in library order, into a single output. Support Markdown, DOCX, HTML, EPUB and PDF. Export runs through a style file the user can edit — fonts, margins, heading treatment, first-line indents, page numbering — because export quality is most of what a writing app is judged on. Ship two styles, a manuscript format and a book format.

Storage: plain Markdown files in a folder the user chooses, plus a rebuildable SQLite index for search and filters. External edits are detected and re-indexed. Never store the only copy of anything in a database.

Version history: snapshot each sheet on a timer and on export, kept in a sidecar directory, restorable from inside the app.

Out of scope: sync of any kind, mobile apps, collaboration, publishing integrations, and any AI feature.

faq.q: Can I get my Ulysses library out?
faq.a: Yes, completely. Ulysses exports the whole library as Markdown files preserving the group structure, and this build reads exactly that. Keywords and goals do not come across and have to be re-applied, which for a large library is the tedious part.

Because Ulysses has none, and adding one would be reviewing a different product. The catalogue has several entries where an AI writing loop is the point; this is the one where the answer is a quiet editor and a good export pipeline.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing. Local files, a local index, no keys, no server. Your writing never leaves the machine, which for some people is the entire argument.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Sync you can trust. Ulysses moves a library between a Mac, an iPad and an iPhone without you thinking about it. Putting a Markdown folder in a sync service mostly works and occasionally produces conflict copies mid-chapter, which is a bad day for a writer.
